comparison: Perfect agreement on clustering enhancement claims (C7, C27, C28). Both evaluations find the evidence for acetylation-enhanced vesicle clustering strongly supported by DLS and TEM data. Editor and reviewers affirmed this as a core finding with solid evidence.

Perfect agreement on LPC-specific clustering enhancement (C30, C31, C32). Both evaluations accept the differential lipid effects showing LPC specificity over DOPS, with no concerns raised about the data quality or interpretation.

Strong agreement on NMR binding data (C34-C38, C40). Both evaluations view the residue-resolved NMR structural characterization as a major strength, showing differential binding patterns and enhanced N-terminal affinity to LPC. Peer reviewers explicitly praised this structural work.

Agreement on physiological acetylation claims (C5, C24, C25, C26). Both evaluations accept the in-cell NMR evidence for spontaneous acetylation under physiological conditions. OpenEval also includes C6 and C23 regarding irreversibility and chemical shift data, which were not explicitly addressed by peer reviewers but not challenged.

Agreement on native SV binding data (C41, C42, C43). OpenEval finds these claims well-supported by NMR with native SVs. Peer reviewers grouped these with other NMR structural data (R4) and praised the demonstration of N-terminal involvement, viewing it as a strength.

Agreement on cross-linking data (C46, C47, C48, C56). Both evaluations accept the XL-MS evidence for increased intermolecular interactions. OpenEval also includes C8, C9 regarding N-terminal insertion mechanism, which peer reviewers accepted as part of the broader mechanistic interpretation (see R7).

Agreement on mechanistic integration (C10, C52, C61). Both evaluations accept the mechanistic interpretation linking N-terminal insertion, charge neutralization, and intermolecular interactions to clustering. OpenEval notes these are higher-level interpretations; peer reviewers accepted them as supported by convergent structural and biochemical data.

Agreement on modest DOPS effects (C39, C40). Both evaluations accept the NMR data showing only slight weakening of DOPS binding with acetylation. Peer reviewers noted no difference was observed with phosphatidylserine, aligning with the 'modest' characterization.

Partial overlap on charge neutralization mechanism (C54, C55, C65, C66, C67). OpenEval finds these mechanistic interpretations supported but inferential. Peer reviewers accepted the DOPS data (C55, C66, C67 relate to charge effects) without challenge, though they questioned broader physiological relevance.

Partial overlap on regional availability model (C65). OpenEval includes this in mechanistic interpretations supported by NMR and XL-MS. Peer reviewers accepted the cross-linking evidence for increased intermolecular interactions that underlies this model.

Agreement on uncertainty of physiological speculation (C62, C63, C64). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative proposals requiring future validation. Peer reviewers similarly expressed uncertainty about physiological relevance, particularly regarding pathological conditions and LPC interactions.

Partial overlap on background literature (C2, C57, C58, C59). OpenEval identifies these as established background knowledge from prior literature. Peer reviewers questioned the physiological relevance of LPC interactions (R8), which relates to the broader context these background claims establish.

Minimal overlap on knowledge gaps (C60). OpenEval identifies this as a knowledge gap motivating the study. Peer reviewers accepted the evidence addressing this gap regarding physiological acetylation, though they raised new questions about LPC physiological relevance.

OpenEval identified extensive background claims (C1-C21, C29, C33, C44-C45, C49, C51, C53) as supported by prior literature. These contextual claims were not explicitly evaluated by peer reviewers, who focused on novel findings and their physiological significance.

OpenEval identified knowledge gaps (C3, C4, C22, C50) that motivated the study. Peer reviewers did not explicitly evaluate these framing statements, focusing instead on whether the new data addressed relevant biological questions.

Peer reviewers raised significant concerns about physiological relevance of LPC interactions that extend beyond specific claims. While they accepted the in vitro findings, they questioned whether LPC concentrations and interactions are physiologically meaningful, representing a broader evaluative dimension not captured in OpenEval's claim-by-claim assessment.
